content.title: UConn women’s basketball shares close ties to Syracuse coaches, players in NCAA Tournament matchup
content.text: STORRS — The first time Geno Auriemma met Syracuse coach Felisha Legette-Jack, he was a 30-year-old assistant at Virginia trying to convince the teenage center to play for the Cavaliers. Legette-Jack entertained Virginia’s interest in part because her high school coach thought Auriemma was, “the most handsome guy she ever saw in her life,” and insisted that she consider his offer. When she took her visit to Charlottesville, she said she barely saw Cavaliers head coach Debby Ryan. It was Auriemma who took her on the tour around campus and made the official recruiting pitch. Legette-Jack, a Syracuse, N.Y. native, ultimately committed to her hometown team over Virginia, but it wasn’t the last she’d see of Auriemma. After her freshman year with the Orange, Auriemma was hired ahead of the 1985-86 season to lead the UConn women’s basketball team — a Big East rival of Syracuse. The Orange were dominant in the series at the time, and Legette-Jack graduated with a 4-1 record in games she played against Auriemma’s Huskies. “It just didn’t feel right to leave and go to that color orange when I’ve got Syracuse right in my backyard, so I decided to stay home,” Legette-Jack said with a smile Sunday. “It was kind of a blessing, because he ended up taking the job here, so that’s how long we’ve known each other … One thing I love about Geno, he’s a loyal human being. Once he locks in to believing in you and what you bring, you can mess up a couple times, and he’ll still forgive you, because his loyalty is real.” Legette-Jack stayed in touch with Auriemma even after her playing career ended, and the Hall of Famer has become a mentor for her since she entered the coaching world. Legette-Jack spent stints as an assistant at Boston College, Syracuse and Michigan State before taking her first head coaching gig at Hofstra in 2002. She went on to coach Indiana from 2006-12, then spent a decade leading Buffalo before returning to her alma mater. Auriemma says he called former Syracuse athletic director John Wildhack to endorse hiring Legette-Jack as head coach when the job opened in 2022. On Monday, Auriemma’s undefeated No. 1 Huskies will face Legette-Jack’s 9-seed Orange in the second round of the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 6 p.m. at Gampel Pavilion. It’s the second time the programs have met during March Madness since Legette-Jack took over at Syracuse, and though Auriemma knows the matchup will be a challenge, he’s excited to see her team have success in the postseason. “I’m really proud of her,” Auriemma said. “She got an opportunity at Indiana, and it didn’t pan out. A lot of times when things like that happen, a lot of young coaches get buried and they never have an opportunity. They kind of have to work their way up through mid-majors and they never get another chance. I’m incredibly thrilled that she had an opportunity to get back to that level, and she’s made the most of it.” Former AAU teammates go head-to-head According to Syracuse guard Shy Hawkins, UConn sophomore Kayleigh Heckel is the only player she’s ever met who can keep up with her in a foot race. “She’s always been very fast, and I was a fast one too,” Hawkins said. “She was the only one to always challenge me to race. She’s very competitive but she’s fun and very funny. It’s always a good time with her.” “I’m faster,” Heckel added with a smirk. “Sometimes she’d be like ‘Oh I wasn’t trying,’ or something. But like, whatever. I used to win them, mostly.” Hawkins and Heckel first met while playing for Exodus EYBL, an elite AAU program based out of New York City. The became fast friends and also played a year of high school basketball together at Long Island Lutheran. The pair remained close even after committing to different colleges, and they keep in touch frequently via FaceTime. Heckel said they got a chance to hang out in person at Mohegan Sun in November when Syracuse and UConn were both competing in the Basketball Hall of Fame Classic — though not against each other. Hawkins joked that Heckel is usually the instigator of any trash talk between them, but there hasn’t been much jawing ahead of Monday’s second-round NCAA Tournament game. “I loved playing with Shy,” Heckel said. “She’s hilarious. When I played with her we were always close, and it was always super fun playing with her because she’s super athletic. I feel like we always had a really good connection on the court, so I’m happy to see how much she’s grown and how she’s doing now … It’s just cool to be able to see her again” UConn’s Ducharme is ‘role model’ for Syracuse freshman When Syracuse freshman Jasmyn Cooper was coming up through the youth basketball circuit in eastern Massachusetts, UConn senior Caroline Ducharme was one of the biggest names in the area. Ducharme, a Milton, Mass. native, committed to the Huskies as the No. 5 prospect in the Class of 2021, and Cooper always admired the older guard from afar as a middle schooler dreaming of taking her game to that level. “She was this great shooter, and she was a great teammate. She was able to move the ball well, shoot it, take the right shots,” Cooper said. “She’s always just been a role model, but now us both being in college, it’s definitely a weird experience but also fun and unique.” Cooper and Ducharme never shared the court because of their age difference, but Ducharme spent several seasons in the same AAU program as Cooper, and both attended Noble & Greenough in Dedham, Mass. for high school. Ducharme still remembers Cooper as an eager tween, and it’s hard to reconcile the little girl she grew up with with the 6-foot-1 Division I basketball player set to take the court against UConn tomorrow in the NCAA Tournament. “It’s been crazy to see her grow up,” Ducharme said. “I remember watching her when she was probably in like fifth grade, and I would go to their practices to help out … Her whole team, that little baby team, I still think of them like they’re 12 … but I’m not surprised that they were able to produce so many great players, and it’s just a testament to her and how hard she’s worked.” After she started at UConn, Ducharme would occasionally stop by a practice and speak with the team when she was home from college. Cooper hung onto every word, and in her first March Madness experience, she’s still carrying that advice. “Just staying ready and doing your part,” Cooper said Ducharme told the younger players. “Transferring from high school to college is a very different experience, and your role in high school will be much different in college, so just buying into that and trusting the process in whatever program you’re in.”
